topics.name: Integrals
topics.kicker: The area under a curve · The reverse of taking a derivative
topics.dates: ∫ sign first written by Gottfried Leibniz, 1675
topics.briefing: An integral adds up infinitely many tiny pieces to find a total, like the area under a curve or the distance a car travels when its speed keeps changing. Integration is the reverse of differentiation: the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus links the two, so knowing a function’s antiderivative lets you compute areas exactly. Its tall, curvy symbol, ∫, is a stretched-out S that Gottfried Leibniz chose to stand for “sum.”
topics.answerHtml: integrals (or integration; prompt on antiderivatives or area under the curve; do not accept “derivative”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Gottfried Leibniz first wrote this operation’s symbol in 1675, choosing a tall, stretched-out letter S to stand for the Latin word for “sum.” The “dx” written at the end of that notation stands for the width of an extremely thin slice.
tossups.r: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus says this operation undoes differentiation. For 10 points, name this calculus operation used to find the area under a curve.

tossups.p: Gaston Darboux [“dar-BOO”] defined this operation by squeezing it between upper and lower sums. Bernhard Riemann [“REE-mahn”] defined it as the limit of sums of the areas of thin rectangles, whose heights can be taken at the left end, right end, or middle of each slice.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus operation that finds the area under a curve, the reverse of taking a derivative.

tossups.p: Isaac Barrow, Isaac Newton’s teacher, proved an early version of a theorem saying that this operation and differentiation undo each other. That theorem says the definite form of this operation from a to b equals F of b minus F of a, where F is an antiderivative.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus operation, written with a long S, that finds the area under a curve.

tossups.p: Archimedes used the method of exhaustion, an ancient forerunner of this operation, to show that a slice of a parabola has four-thirds the area of a certain triangle inside it. Bonaventura Cavalieri’s “method of indivisibles” was another early version of this operation.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus operation that adds up infinitely many tiny pieces to find an area.

tossups.p: This operation applied to the bell-shaped curve e to the negative x squared, over the whole number line, gives the square root of pi. That curve has no antiderivative made of ordinary functions, so mathematicians define a special “error function” for it.
tossups.r: It is the reverse of taking a derivative. For 10 points, name this calculus operation that finds the area under a curve.

tossups.p: One method for this operation, done “by parts,” comes from the product rule and turns it into u v minus the same operation on v d u. Another method, u-substitution, reverses the chain rule, and partial fractions help with this operation on rational functions.
tossups.r: It is the reverse of differentiation. For 10 points, name this calculus operation that finds antiderivatives and areas under curves.

tossups.p: Henri Lebesgue [“luh-BEG”] created a more powerful version of this operation in 1902 by measuring the sets where a function takes its values. Fubini’s [“foo-BEE-neez”] theorem lets a double version of this operation be done one variable at a time.
tossups.r: Riemann sums approximate it with thin rectangles. For 10 points, name this calculus operation, the reverse of differentiation.

tossups.p: The indefinite form of this operation always ends with “plus C,” because functions that differ only by a constant have the same derivative. For example, doing this operation on 2x gives x squared plus C.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus operation, which finds antiderivatives and the area under a curve.

tossups.p: The disk and shell methods use this operation to find the volume of a solid made by spinning a flat region around an axis. Doing this operation on the difference between two functions finds the area of the region between their curves.
tossups.r: This operation reverses the derivative. For 10 points, name this calculus operation, written with an elongated S.

tossups.p: Evangelista Torricelli first studied Gabriel’s horn, made by spinning the graph of 1 over x, for x of at least 1, around the x-axis; this operation shows it has finite volume but infinite surface area. Versions of this operation over an infinitely long interval are called “improper.”
tossups.r: Its answer can be checked by taking a derivative. For 10 points, name this calculus operation, which finds areas under curves.

tossups.p: Green’s theorem turns this operation taken around a closed curve into this operation over the flat region inside that curve. In physics, applying this operation to a force over a distance gives the work done.
tossups.r: Leibniz and Newton both developed it. For 10 points, name this calculus operation that finds the area under a curve.

tossups.p: Isaac Newton called the quantities found by this operation “fluents,” since he saw this operation as reversing his method of “fluxions.” Numerical methods for estimating this operation’s value are often called “quadrature,” an old word for finding an area.
tossups.r: Its definite form gives a number, while its indefinite form gives a family of functions. For 10 points, name this calculus operation that is the inverse of differentiation.

tossups.p: The average value of a function on an interval equals this operation applied to the function over that interval, divided by the interval’s length. Simpson’s rule estimates this operation using pieces of parabolas, while the trapezoidal rule uses trapezoids.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus operation, which can find the area under a curve.

tossups.p: The probability that a continuous random variable lands between two values is found by applying this operation to its probability density function. Applying this operation to a graph of a car’s speed over time gives the distance the car travels.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus operation that finds the area under a curve.

tossups.p: The Fourier transform, which turns a signal in time into its frequencies, is defined using this operation, as is the Laplace transform. Leonhard Euler wrote the gamma function, which extends factorials, using this operation.
tossups.r: Its symbol is a stretched-out S. For 10 points, name this calculus operation used to compute areas under curves.

The reverse of differentiation (taking a derivative); an indefinite one is an antiderivative
Written with a tall, stretched-out S (∫) that stands for “sum”
Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: from a to b, it equals F(b) − F(a), where F is an antiderivative
Riemann sums estimate it with thin rectangles; taking the limit gives the exact value
An indefinite one ends with “+ C,” since functions that differ by a constant have the same derivative
A definite one has limits a and b and gives a number; an indefinite one gives a family of functions
Calculus was developed independently by Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz in the late 1600s
Techniques: u-substitution (reverses the chain rule), “by parts” (from the product rule), and partial fractions
Speed over time gives the distance traveled; force over a distance gives the work done
The disk and shell methods find volumes of solids made by spinning a region around an axis
The area between two curves comes from doing it on the difference of the two functions
Estimated by the trapezoidal rule and by Simpson’s rule, which uses pieces of parabolas
A function’s average value on an interval is this over the interval, divided by the interval’s length
Gottfried Leibniz first wrote its ∫ symbol in 1675, from the Latin summa; the dx stands for a thin slice’s width
Archimedes’ method of exhaustion was an ancient forerunner; he showed a parabola slice is 4/3 of a triangle inside it
Bonaventura Cavalieri’s “method of indivisibles” was another early version
Isaac Barrow, Newton’s teacher, proved an early version of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
Newton called its results “fluents,” the reverse of his “fluxions”; numerical methods for it are called quadrature
Gaston Darboux defined it by squeezing it between upper and lower sums
Henri Lebesgue’s 1902 version measures the sets where a function takes its values instead of slicing the x-axis
Fubini’s theorem lets a double one be done one variable at a time
Over the whole number line, e^(−x²) gives √π; that curve has no ordinary antiderivative, so the error function is defined for it
Gabriel’s horn, studied by Evangelista Torricelli, has finite volume but infinite surface area; ones over infinite intervals are “improper”
Green’s theorem turns one around a closed curve into one over the region inside it
The Laplace and Fourier transforms, and Euler’s gamma function, are all defined with it
Doing it on a probability density function gives the chance of landing in a range of values

trap.title: Derivative or its reverse?
trap.body: Derivatives and integrals are partners, and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus shows up in tossups on both. Derivatives measure slope or instantaneous rate of change, while integrals measure area or accumulation, so mixing them up is the most common mistake. Some tossups want “Riemann sums” or “limits,” which are tools used to define an integral rather than the integral itself.
trap.fix: Listen for the key words: “slope,” “tangent line,” or “rate of change” mean derivative; “area under a curve,” “antiderivative,” “accumulation,” or the long S symbol mean integral. “Integration” is also accepted, but “antiderivative” alone earns a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: integrals (or integration; prompt on antiderivatives or area under the curve; do not accept “derivative”)

topics.name: Polynomials
topics.kicker: Sums of terms like 3x² − 5x + 2 · The degree limits the number of roots
topics.dates: Fundamental theorem of algebra proved in Gauss’s 1799 thesis
topics.briefing: A polynomial is an expression built from a variable and numbers using only addition, subtraction, multiplication, and whole-number exponents, like 3x² − 5x + 2. Its degree, the highest exponent, tells you a lot: a degree-2, or quadratic, polynomial graphs as a parabola and has at most two real roots. The values that make a polynomial equal zero, called its zeros or roots, are where its graph meets the x-axis.
topics.answerHtml: polynomials (accept specific kinds, such as quadratic polynomials; prompt on expressions or functions; do not accept “roots” or “zeros”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The Abel–Ruffini theorem proves that no general formula using only arithmetic and radicals, such as square roots and cube roots, can find the zeros of these expressions once their degree is five or higher. Évariste Galois [“gal-WAH”] explained exactly which ones of these can be solved that way.
tossups.r: The zeros of quadratic ones of these can be found with the quadratic formula. For 10 points, name these expressions, such as x squared plus 3x plus 2.

tossups.p: Carl Friedrich Gauss’s 1799 doctoral thesis gave a proof that every one of these that is not constant has at least one complex root, a result now called the fundamental theorem of algebra. As a result, one of these of degree n has exactly n complex roots, counting repeats.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these expressions, such as 2x cubed minus x plus 7, whose degree is their highest exponent.

tossups.p: Gerolamo Cardano’s 1545 book _Ars Magna_ published methods for finding the roots of these expressions of degree 3 and 4, angering Niccolò Tartaglia [“tar-TAHL-yah”], who had shared his method for degree 3. Cardano’s student Lodovico Ferrari found the method for degree 4.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these algebraic expressions made of terms like 5x squared, which are classified by their degree.

tossups.p: René Descartes’s rule of signs uses how many times the coefficients of one of these change between positive and negative to limit how many positive real roots it can have. The rational root theorem lists the only fractions that could be roots of one of these with whole-number coefficients.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these expressions, such as x squared minus 4, built from terms with whole-number exponents.

tossups.p: The Weierstrass [“VY-er-shtrahss”] approximation theorem says that any continuous function on a closed interval can be approximated as closely as you like by one of these. Taylor’s theorem approximates a smooth function near a point using one of these built from its derivatives.
tossups.r: Their degree is the highest power of the variable. For 10 points, name these expressions, such as linear, quadratic, and cubic ones.

tossups.p: Joseph-Louis Lagrange gave a formula for the one of these with the lowest possible degree that passes through a given set of points. Any n plus 1 points with different x-coordinates lie on the graph of exactly one of these of degree at most n.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these expressions, like x squared plus 2x plus 1, whose degree is their highest power.

tossups.p: The remainder theorem says that dividing one of these by x minus a leaves a remainder equal to its value at a. Synthetic division is a shortcut for dividing one of these by a linear factor like x minus 3.
tossups.r: If its value at a is zero, then x minus a is a factor. For 10 points, name these expressions, such as x cubed minus 1.

tossups.p: Formulas named for François Viète [“frahn-SWAH vee-ET”] link the coefficients of one of these to the sums and products of its roots. For example, the roots of x squared minus 5x plus 6, which are 2 and 3, add up to 5 and multiply to 6.
tossups.r: One with three terms is a trinomial. For 10 points, name these algebraic expressions whose highest exponent is called their degree.

tossups.p: Computer scientists say a problem is in the class P if it can be solved in an amount of time bounded by one of these functions of the input’s size. Bernstein ones of these are used to draw the smooth Bézier [“BEZ-ee-ay”] curves found in computer fonts and drawing programs.
tossups.r: A quadratic one of these graphs as a parabola. For 10 points, name these expressions built from terms like 4x cubed.

tossups.p: The graph of one of these of degree n can have at most n minus 1 turning points, and its end behavior depends only on its leading term. A cubic one of these, with real coefficients, always crosses the x-axis at least once.
tossups.r: Their zeros are where their graphs meet the x-axis. For 10 points, name these expressions, which include quadratics and cubics.

tossups.p: Pafnuty Chebyshev [“cheh-bih-SHOFF”], Adrien-Marie Legendre [“luh-ZHAHN-druh”], and Charles Hermite [“air-MEET”] each name a famous family of these expressions. The characteristic one of these for a square matrix has the matrix’s eigenvalues as its roots.
tossups.r: One with a single term is a monomial. For 10 points, name these expressions built by adding terms like 7x to the fourth power.

tossups.p: Al-Khwarizmi [“al-KWAR-iz-mee”] solved equations built from these expressions in a book whose title gave us the word “algebra.” The discriminant, b squared minus 4ac, tells whether a degree-2 one of these has two real roots, one repeated real root, or two non-real complex roots.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these expressions, such as x squared plus 2x minus 8, built from terms with whole-number exponents.

tossups.p: Multiplying two binomials with the FOIL method, short for First, Outer, Inner, Last, always produces another one of these expressions. The degree of the product of two of these is the sum of their degrees.
tossups.r: Their zeros are also called roots. For 10 points, name these expressions, which include monomials, binomials, and trinomials.

tossups.p: Horner’s method evaluates one of these quickly by rewriting it as a chain of nested multiplications, a technique the Chinese mathematician Qin Jiushao [“chin jyoh-SHOW”] described centuries before William Horner. Completing the square rewrites one of these, x squared plus 6x plus 5, as the quantity x plus 3, squared, minus 4.
tossups.r: Long division works on them too. For 10 points, name these expressions, whose degree is the highest power of their variable.

tossups.p: The Persian poet and mathematician Omar Khayyam [“OH-mar ky-YAHM”] solved cubic equations built from these expressions by intersecting conic sections. When a zero of one of these is repeated an even number of times, its graph just touches the x-axis there instead of crossing it.
tossups.r: The highest exponent in one of these is its degree. For 10 points, name these expressions, such as 3x squared minus 5x plus 2.

clues.t: Expressions built from a variable and numbers using only +, −, ×, and whole-number exponents, like 3x² − 5x + 2
The degree is the highest exponent: linear (1), quadratic (2), cubic (3), quartic (4), quintic (5)
By number of terms: monomial (1), binomial (2), trinomial (3)
Their zeros, also called roots, are the x-values that make them equal 0, where the graph meets the x-axis
Quadratic formula: x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) ÷ 2a finds the roots of ax² + bx + c
Discriminant b² − 4ac: positive means two real roots, zero means one repeated root, negative means two non-real roots
Fundamental theorem of algebra: one of degree n has exactly n complex roots, counting repeats (Gauss, 1799)
Remainder theorem: dividing by x − a leaves its value at a; factor theorem: if that value is 0, x − a is a factor
Synthetic division and long division divide one by a linear factor like x − 3
FOIL (First, Outer, Inner, Last) multiplies two binomials; a product’s degree is the sum of the two degrees
Rational root theorem: any fraction root is ± (a factor of the constant term) ÷ (a factor of the leading coefficient)
A degree-n one has at most n − 1 turning points; its leading term sets the end behavior; a quadratic one graphs as a parabola
Vieta’s formulas: for x² − 5x + 6, the roots 2 and 3 add to 5 and multiply to 6
An odd-degree one with real coefficients, like a cubic, always crosses the x-axis at least once; at a zero repeated an even number of times, it only touches the axis
Abel–Ruffini theorem: no general formula using arithmetic and roots (radicals) solves them at degree 5 or higher
Évariste Galois explained exactly which ones can be solved with radicals
Cardano’s _Ars Magna_ (1545) published solutions for degrees 3 and 4, angering Tartaglia; Ferrari found the degree-4 method
Descartes’ rule of signs limits the number of positive real roots by counting sign changes in the coefficients
Weierstrass approximation theorem: any continuous function on a closed interval can be approximated as closely as you like by one
Taylor ones approximate a smooth function near a point using its derivatives
Lagrange interpolation finds the lowest-degree one through given points; n + 1 points fix one of degree at most n
Famous families are named for Chebyshev, Legendre, and Hermite; a square matrix’s characteristic one has its eigenvalues as roots
A problem is in the class P if it can be solved in time bounded by one of these functions of the input size
Bernstein ones define the Bézier curves used in computer fonts and drawing programs
Horner’s method evaluates one with nested multiplication; Qin Jiushao described it centuries earlier
Completing the square rewrites x² + 6x + 5 as (x + 3)² − 4, the same method used to derive the quadratic formula
The Persian poet and mathematician Omar Khayyam solved cubic equations by intersecting conic sections
Al-Khwarizmi solved quadratic equations in a book whose title (al-jabr) gave us the word “algebra”

trap.title: The expression or its zeros?
trap.body: Many tossups about polynomials actually ask for their zeros, also called roots: the x-values that make the polynomial equal 0, where its graph meets the x-axis. A question built on the quadratic formula or the fundamental theorem of algebra may want “roots” rather than “polynomials.” Others want one named piece, such as the discriminant or the quadratic formula itself.
trap.fix: Listen to the noun. “These expressions” or “these functions,” with clues about degree and terms, means polynomials; “these values” or “these numbers” that make one equal zero means zeros or roots. Answering only “expression” or “function” earns a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: polynomials (accept specific kinds, such as quadratic polynomials; prompt on expressions or functions)

topics.name: Carl Friedrich Gauss
topics.kicker: German “Prince of Mathematicians” · Number theory, Ceres, and the bell curve
topics.briefing: Carl Friedrich Gauss was a German mathematician so brilliant that he is called the “Prince of Mathematicians.” A famous story says that as a schoolboy he added up the numbers from 1 to 100 in moments by pairing them into fifty sums of 101. He went on to show how to draw a regular 17-sided polygon with just a compass and straightedge, help astronomers find the lost dwarf planet Ceres, and lend his name to the bell curve.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Daniel Kehlmann’s [“KAYL-mahnz”] novel _Measuring the World_ follows this man and the explorer Alexander von Humboldt. This man’s motto, “Pauca sed matura” [“POW-kuh sed mah-TOO-ruh”], meaning “few, but ripe,” explains why he published only work he had polished.
tossups.r: As a schoolboy, he reportedly added up the numbers from 1 to 100 in moments. For 10 points, name this German “Prince of Mathematicians.”

tossups.p: A unit of magnetic flux density equal to one ten-thousandth of a tesla is named for this man. In 1833, he and the physicist Wilhelm Weber [“VAY-ber”] built one of the first electromagnetic telegraphs, sending signals across the town of Göttingen [“GUHT-ing-un”].
tossups.r: The normal distribution, or bell curve, is often named for him. For 10 points, name this German mathematician.

tossups.p: This man’s Theorema Egregium [“ih-GREE-jee-um”], or “Remarkable Theorem,” shows that the curvature of a surface can be measured without leaving the surface. One result is that no flat map of the round Earth can show every distance correctly.
tossups.r: He directed the observatory at Göttingen [“GUHT-ing-un”] for nearly fifty years. For 10 points, name this German mathematician who proved the fundamental theorem of algebra in his 1799 doctoral thesis.

tossups.p: When the newly found dwarf planet Ceres disappeared into the Sun’s glare in 1801, this man calculated its orbit so well that astronomers found it again close to where he predicted. His 1809 book on the motion of heavenly bodies explained his method of least squares.
tossups.r: As a boy, he supposedly summed the numbers from 1 to 100 almost instantly. For 10 points, name this “Prince of Mathematicians.”

tossups.p: The first entry in this man’s math diary records his 1796 discovery that a regular 17-sided polygon can be drawn with just a compass and straightedge. In a famous story, he wanted that shape on his tombstone, but the stonecutter refused, saying it would look like a circle.
tossups.r: As a boy, he quickly added the numbers from 1 to 100 by pairing them. For 10 points, name this German “Prince of Mathematicians.”

tossups.p: In 1796, this man wrote “Eureka” in Greek letters in his diary after proving that every positive whole number is the sum of at most three triangular numbers. His 1801 book _Disquisitiones Arithmeticae_ [“dis-kwiz-ih-tee-OH-nays ar-ith-MET-ih-kye”] introduced the three-line symbol for congruence in modular arithmetic.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German mathematician who, as a schoolboy, famously added the numbers from 1 to 100.

tossups.p: Sophie Germain [“zhair-MAN”] sent this man her discoveries in number theory under the false name “Monsieur LeBlanc.” When French troops occupied his hometown of Brunswick in 1806, she asked a French general to make sure he was safe.
tossups.r: He later used a bell-shaped curve to describe errors in measurements. For 10 points, name this German mathematician.

tossups.p: When his old friend Farkas Bolyai [“BOH-yoy”] sent him the new geometry of his son János, which rejects Euclid’s parallel postulate, this man replied that praising it would mean praising himself, since he had reached the same ideas years earlier without publishing them.
tossups.r: The bell curve is often named for him. For 10 points, name this German mathematician who found the sum of the numbers from 1 to 100 as a boy.

tossups.p: While surveying the Kingdom of Hanover, this man invented the heliotrope, a device that uses a mirror to flash sunlight toward faraway survey stations. That survey’s careful measurements of huge triangles led him to study the curvature of surfaces.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German mathematician and astronomer at Göttingen [“GUHT-ing-un”], who is called the “Prince of Mathematicians.”

tossups.p: Before Germany switched to the euro, its 10-mark banknote showed this man’s portrait. In his 1799 doctoral thesis, he gave a proof that every polynomial that is not constant has at least one complex root, a result called the fundamental theorem of algebra.
tossups.r: The normal distribution’s bell curve is often named for him. For 10 points, name this German mathematician.

tossups.p: Adrien-Marie Legendre [“luh-ZHAHN-druh”] published the method of least squares in 1805, but this man claimed that he had used it since 1795, starting a bitter dispute. A method of solving systems of linear equations by row reduction is also named for this man.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mathematician from Brunswick, Germany, who is called the “Prince of Mathematicians.”

tossups.p: This man supervised Bernhard Riemann’s [“REE-mahnz”] doctoral thesis and chose geometry, the last of three topics Riemann offered, for Riemann’s famous 1854 lecture. Richard Dedekind [“DAY-duh-kint”] was also one of this man’s students at Göttingen [“GUHT-ing-un”].
tossups.r: As a teenager, he showed how to construct a regular 17-sided polygon. For 10 points, name this German mathematician.

tossups.p: Numbers of the form a plus b i, in which a and b are both integers, are named for this man, who also popularized the term “complex number.” He gave several different proofs of the law of quadratic reciprocity, which he called the “golden theorem.”
tossups.r: His 1801 book _Disquisitiones Arithmeticae_ [“dis-kwiz-ih-tee-OH-nays ar-ith-MET-ih-kye”] helped found modern number theory. For 10 points, name this German “Prince of Mathematicians.”

tossups.p: This man showed that a regular polygon can be drawn with compass and straightedge whenever its number of sides is a Fermat prime, such as 17, 257, or 65,537. Pierre Wantzel later proved that no other prime numbers of sides work.
tossups.r: He also proved the fundamental theorem of algebra. For 10 points, name this German mathematician who, as a boy, quickly summed the numbers from 1 to 100.

tossups.p: As a teenager, this man guessed how thinly the prime numbers are spread out among larger and larger numbers, a guess proved in 1896. He is often quoted as calling mathematics “the queen of the sciences” and number theory “the queen of mathematics.”
tossups.r: The Duke of Brunswick paid for his education. For 10 points, name this German known as the “Prince of Mathematicians.”

trap.title: Gauss or Euler?
trap.body: Leonhard Euler and Gauss both have dozens of ideas named after them, and both did deep work in number theory, so early clues can fit either one. Other tossups want one of his namesakes instead of the man: Gauss’s law in physics, the normal (“Gaussian”) distribution in statistics, or Gaussian elimination in algebra.
trap.fix: Use the life clues. Gauss was German (Brunswick and Göttingen), summed 1 to 100 as a boy, showed how to construct the 17-sided polygon, and calculated the orbit of Ceres; Euler was Swiss, went nearly blind, and solved the Seven Bridges of Königsberg. If the question asks for “this law,” “this distribution,” or “this method,” name the thing, not the man.

topics.name: Pierre de Fermat
topics.kicker: French lawyer and amateur mathematician · Famous for a note in a margin
topics.briefing: Pierre de Fermat [“fair-MAH”] was a French lawyer who did mathematics in his spare time, yet he helped invent probability, analytic geometry, and modern number theory. Around 1637, he wrote in the margin of an ancient Greek math book that he had a “truly marvelous” proof that the margin was too small to hold. That claim, his “Last Theorem,” stumped mathematicians for more than 350 years, until Andrew Wiles proved it in the 1990s.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In a letter dated Christmas Day, 1640, this man told Marin Mersenne [“mair-SEN”] that an odd prime is a sum of two squares exactly when it is 1 more than a multiple of 4, as 13 is 4 plus 9. Leonhard Euler later published the first proof.
tossups.r: This lawyer did mathematics in his spare time. For 10 points, name this French mathematician whose “Last Theorem” was finally proved by Andrew Wiles.

tossups.p: This man developed the method of infinite descent and used it to prove that no right triangle with whole-number sides can have an area that is a perfect square. That proof settles the fourth-power case of his most famous claim.
tossups.r: He wrote that claim in the margin of a book by Diophantus [“dy-oh-FAN-tus”]. For 10 points, name this French mathematician whose “Last Theorem” went unproven for more than 350 years.

tossups.p: In 1657, this man challenged English mathematicians such as John Wallis to find whole-number solutions to equations of the form x squared minus N y squared equals 1. Leonhard Euler later mistakenly named those equations after John Pell.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French mathematician who wrote that a book’s margin was too narrow to hold his proof.

tossups.p: This man’s method for factoring an odd number writes it as a difference of two squares, as when 91 equals 100 minus 9, which equals 13 times 7. He first stated his “little theorem” about primes in a 1640 letter to Bernard Frénicle de Bessy [“fray-NEE-kluh duh beh-SEE”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French mathematician whose “Last Theorem” says that a to the n plus b to the n never equals c to the n in positive whole numbers for n above 2.

tossups.p: This man served as a councillor in the parlement of Toulouse [“too-LOOZ”], a high court. He challenged Evangelista Torricelli [“tor-ih-CHEL-ee”] to find the point inside a triangle with the smallest total distance to its three corners, a point now named for this man.
tossups.r: In 1654, he and Blaise Pascal [“pass-KAL”] exchanged letters that began probability theory. For 10 points, name this French mathematician.

tossups.p: This man claimed that every positive whole number is the sum of at most three triangular numbers, at most four squares, and at most five pentagonal numbers. Augustin-Louis Cauchy [“koh-SHEE”] finally proved the full claim in 1813, long after this man died without leaving a proof.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French mathematician who said he had a “truly marvelous” proof of his “Last Theorem.”

tossups.p: Five years after this man died in Castres [“KAS-truh”], his son Clément-Samuel published a new edition of an ancient Greek book on number theory that included this man’s own comments on its problems.
tossups.r: One comment claimed a proof too big to fit in the margin. For 10 points, name this French mathematician whose “Last Theorem” Andrew Wiles proved.

tossups.p: This man argued with René Descartes [“day-KART”] about optics and about how to find tangent lines. His principle of least time says that light travels between two points along the path that takes the shortest time, which explains why light bends when it passes from air into water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French mathematician whose “Last Theorem” stumped mathematicians for more than three centuries.

tossups.p: In a manuscript introducing “plane and solid loci,” this man used equations in two unknowns to describe lines, circles, and other curves. He developed that analytic geometry at about the same time as René Descartes [“day-KART”], but independently of him.
tossups.r: This man and Blaise Pascal founded probability theory in their letters. For 10 points, name this French mathematician whose “Last Theorem” Andrew Wiles proved in the 1990s.

tossups.p: Decades before Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz developed calculus, this man found the highest and lowest points of curves and drew their tangent lines with a method he called “adequality.” He did this mathematics only in his spare time, while working as a lawyer.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French “Prince of Amateurs,” whose “Last Theorem” was proved by Andrew Wiles.

tossups.p: This man guessed that every number of the form 2 to the power 2 to the n, plus 1, is prime, which works for 3, 5, 17, 257, and 65,537. Leonhard Euler disproved that guess by showing that 2 to the 32nd power, plus 1, is divisible by 641.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French mathematician, whose “Last Theorem” is about a to the n plus b to the n equaling c to the n.

tossups.p: This man rarely published, sharing his results in letters to friends such as Marin Mersenne [“mair-SEN”]. His “little theorem,” the basis of fast computer tests for prime numbers, says that if p is prime, then a to the p, minus a, is always a multiple of p.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French mathematician whose “Last Theorem” was proved by Andrew Wiles in the 1990s.

tossups.p: After the Chevalier de Méré [“may-RAY”] asked how to split the money from a game of chance that ends early, this man and a fellow Frenchman solved the “problem of points” in a series of 1654 letters.
tossups.r: Those letters with Blaise Pascal [“pass-KAL”] helped found probability theory. For 10 points, name this French mathematician whose “Last Theorem” Andrew Wiles proved.

tossups.p: Born in Beaumont-de-Lomagne [“boh-MOHN duh loh-MAHN-yuh”], this man spent his career as a lawyer and councillor in Toulouse [“too-LOOZ”] and died in Castres [“KAS-truh”] in 1665. He did mathematics only in his spare time and rarely published it.
tossups.r: He is often called the “Prince of Amateurs.” For 10 points, name this French mathematician whose “Last Theorem” Andrew Wiles proved.

tossups.p: A spiral named for this man, with the polar equation r squared equals a squared times theta, is used to model the pattern of seeds in a sunflower head. He also found the areas under curves of the form y equals x to the n.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French mathematician whose “Last Theorem” about whole-number powers was proved by Andrew Wiles.

clues.t: His “Last Theorem”: aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ has no positive whole-number solutions when n > 2; Andrew Wiles proved it in the 1990s

trap.title: The man or his theorem?
trap.body: Pierre de Fermat and his “Last Theorem” are separate answer lines that share almost every clue: the margin of Diophantus’s _Arithmetica_, the “truly marvelous” proof, and Andrew Wiles. Other tossups want one of his namesakes, such as Fermat’s little theorem or Fermat’s principle of least time. Don’t confuse him with Enrico Fermi, a 20th-century physicist.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this man,” “this lawyer,” or “this mathematician” means Pierre de Fermat; “this theorem,” “this statement,” or “this equation” means Fermat’s Last Theorem. Clues about his life, like Toulouse, Pascal, or Mersenne, point to the man.

topics.name: Zero
topics.kicker: Neither positive nor negative · The digit that holds an empty place
topics.dates: First rules for arithmetic with it: Brahmagupta, 628 CE
topics.briefing: Zero stands for “nothing,” but treating nothing as an actual number was a big idea that took centuries to catch on. The Babylonians and the Maya used symbols to mark empty places, and in 628 CE the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta gave rules for adding, subtracting, and multiplying with zero. It is neither positive nor negative, adding it to a number changes nothing, and dividing by it is undefined.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 628 CE, the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta [“BRAH-muh-GOOP-tuh”] gave the first known rules for arithmetic with this number, such as the rule that a number minus itself equals this number. He wrongly claimed that this number divided by itself also equals this number.
tossups.r: Dividing any number by it is undefined. For 10 points, name this number, which is neither positive nor negative.

tossups.p: The Bakhshali [“bahk-SHAH-lee”] manuscript, found buried in a field in 1881 in what is now Pakistan, uses a dot to stand for this number. In Sanskrit, this number was called shunya [“SHOON-yuh”], a word meaning “empty.”
tossups.r: Adding this number to any number leaves that number unchanged. For 10 points, name this number, the additive identity.

tossups.p: The Maya wrote this number with a shell-shaped symbol in their Long Count calendar. Babylonian scribes, who counted in base 60, used two slanted wedges to mark the empty place this number fills inside a numeral.
tossups.r: Multiplying any number by it gives this number. For 10 points, name this number that sits halfway between negative 1 and 1.

tossups.p: In the 800s CE, al-Khwarizmi [“al-KWAR-iz-mee”] explained the Indian numerals, including a symbol for this number, to readers in the Islamic world. Fibonacci’s 1202 book _Liber Abaci_ brought those numerals to Europe and wrote that this digit is called zephirum.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this digit, which holds an empty place in numbers like 105.

tossups.p: An inscription from 876 CE in a temple at Gwalior [“GWAH-lee-or”], India, writes the number 270 with a small circle for this number. The English word “cipher” comes from sifr, the Arabic name for this number, which meant “empty.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number, written as a circle, that is the only number neither positive nor negative.

tossups.p: Charles Seife’s 2000 book subtitled _The Biography of a Dangerous Idea_ tells the story of this number. Roman numerals have no symbol for this number, which reached Europe through Arabic writings in the Middle Ages.
tossups.r: Subtracting any number from itself gives this number. For 10 points, name this number, the additive identity.

tossups.p: The calendar used for BCE and CE dates has no year with this number, so 1 BCE is followed directly by 1 CE. Astronomers, however, count years using a system that does include a year with this number.
tossups.r: Water freezes at this many degrees on the Celsius scale. For 10 points, name this number, which is neither positive nor negative.

tossups.p: In many programming languages, including C and Python, the first item in a list has this index, a choice that computer scientist Edsger Dijkstra [“DYKE-struh”] defended in a 1982 note. Binary code writes every number using only 1 and this digit.
tossups.r: In tennis, a score of this number is called “love.” For 10 points, name this smallest whole number.

tossups.p: The factorial of this number is defined to equal 1, and any number other than this one raised to this power also equals 1. This number counts as even, because dividing it by 2 leaves no remainder.
tossups.r: It is the only number equal to its own opposite. For 10 points, name this number, which is neither positive nor negative.

tossups.p: In his _Almagest_, the Greek astronomer Ptolemy [“TOL-uh-mee”] used a small circle with a long bar over it to stand for this number in his tables, which counted in base 60, as the Babylonians had.
tossups.r: Without a symbol for this number, the numerals for 15 and 105 would look the same. For 10 points, name this number, the additive identity.

tossups.p: The Indian mathematician Mahavira [“muh-HAH-vee-ruh”] wrongly wrote that dividing a number by this number leaves the number unchanged, and centuries later Bhaskara II [“BAHS-kuh-ruh”] said that such a division produces an infinite amount.
tossups.r: A horizontal line has a slope equal to this number. For 10 points, name this number, which is neither positive nor negative.

tossups.p: Leonhard Euler’s famous identity says that e to the i pi, plus 1, equals this number. The empty set, which is written as a circle with a slash through it, has this many elements.
tossups.r: Both coordinates of the origin on a graph equal this number. For 10 points, name this number, the additive identity.

tossups.p: A stone inscription found at Sambor in Cambodia, dated 683 CE, uses a dot for this number when writing the year 605. It is one of the oldest dated examples of a written symbol for this number.
tossups.r: Any number times this number equals this number. For 10 points, name this number.

tossups.p: Gottfried Leibniz’s 1703 paper on binary arithmetic, which writes every number using only 1 and this digit, compared that system to the hexagrams of the ancient Chinese _I Ching_. In a computer circuit, this binary digit usually stands for “off.”
tossups.r: The Prime Meridian has a longitude of this many degrees. For 10 points, name this digit.

tossups.p: In 1997, the U.S. Navy cruiser _Yorktown_ lost engine power after a computer program tried to divide by this number. Such a division has no answer, because multiplying this number by anything gives only this number.
tossups.r: On the Kelvin scale, the coldest possible temperature has this value. For 10 points, name this number.

trap.title: Not one, not infinity
trap.body: Several clues about this number mention the number 1 (its factorial is 1, and any other number raised to its power is 1), so players who buzz on the last number they heard say “one.” Clues about dividing by it can pull players toward “infinity.” Some tossups want a related answer line instead, such as absolute zero (the coldest temperature), the empty set, or the zeros of a function.
trap.fix: Ask which number the clue is about, not which number it mentions. “Neither positive nor negative,” “additive identity,” “placeholder,” Brahmagupta, or shunya means zero. If the giveaway asks for a temperature or a set, answer absolute zero or the empty set instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: zero (or 0; accept nought or naught; prompt on nothing or none)

topics.name: Fractals
topics.kicker: Shapes whose small parts look like the whole · Named by Benoit Mandelbrot
topics.briefing: A fractal is a shape whose small parts look like the whole, so zooming in reveals the same patterns again and again, like the florets of Romanesco broccoli or the branches of a fern. Mathematician Benoit Mandelbrot coined the name in 1975 from the Latin word for “broken.” Some fractals, like the Koch snowflake, even fit a boundary of infinite length around a finite area.
topics.answerHtml: fractals (accept fractal geometry; prompt on self-similar shapes; do not accept a single example such as “Mandelbrot set”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The Hausdorff [“HOWS-dorf”] dimension of the Koch curve, one of these shapes, is the logarithm of 4 divided by the logarithm of 3, or about 1.26. Joining three copies of that 1904 curve by Helge von Koch makes a “snowflake” that encloses a finite area with a boundary of infinite length.
tossups.r: These shapes show self-similarity, meaning that their small parts look like the whole. For 10 points, name these never-ending patterns, which were named by Benoit Mandelbrot.

tossups.p: Lewis Fry Richardson noticed that the measured lengths of coastlines and borders keep growing as the measuring stick gets shorter. A famous 1967 paper built on that idea by asking “How Long Is the Coast of Britain?”
tossups.r: That paper’s author, Benoit Mandelbrot [“ben-WAH MAN-dul-broht”], later named these shapes from the Latin word for “broken.” For 10 points, name these self-similar shapes.

tossups.p: Karl Menger’s 1926 example of these shapes starts with a cube, removes its center and the middle of each face, and repeats that forever on every smaller cube that remains. The result has infinite surface area but no volume.
tossups.r: The Sierpiński [“sher-PEEN-skee”] triangle and the Koch snowflake are other examples. For 10 points, name these self-similar shapes.

tossups.p: Removing the middle third of a line segment, then the middle thirds of the pieces that remain, forever, produces one of these shapes named for Georg Cantor. That set has dimension log 2 over log 3, about 0.63, but contains uncountably many points.
tossups.r: Benoit Mandelbrot coined the name for these shapes. For 10 points, name these self-similar shapes, whose dimensions are often not whole numbers.

tossups.p: Around 1918, Gaston Julia [“zhoo-LYAH”] and Pierre Fatou [“fah-TOO”] studied what happens when a rule for complex numbers, such as squaring and then adding a constant, is repeated over and over. The sets named for Julia that come out of that process are examples of these shapes.
tossups.r: The Mandelbrot set is another example. For 10 points, name these infinitely detailed, self-similar shapes.

tossups.p: Karl Weierstrass [“VY-er-shtrahss”] described a graph that can be drawn without lifting the pencil but has no tangent line at any point, an early example of these shapes. Giuseppe Peano [“pay-AH-noh”] found another, a curve that passes through every point of a square.
tossups.r: Their dimensions are often not whole numbers. For 10 points, name these self-similar shapes, whose name Benoit Mandelbrot coined in 1975.

tossups.p: Loren Carpenter used these shapes to create realistic mountains for the “Genesis” sequence in the 1982 film _Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan_. Computer artists also use them to draw clouds, coastlines, and trees.
tossups.r: Lightning bolts and river networks also have this branching look. For 10 points, name these self-similar patterns studied by Benoit Mandelbrot.

tossups.p: Michael Barnsley showed how to draw a realistic fern, one of these shapes, by repeating four simple transformations chosen at random. A similar “chaos game,” in which a point jumps halfway toward randomly chosen corners of a triangle, traces out the Sierpiński [“sher-PEEN-skee”] triangle.
tossups.r: These shapes look much the same when you zoom in. For 10 points, name these self-similar shapes made famous by Benoit Mandelbrot.

tossups.p: Coloring every odd number in Pascal’s triangle reveals one of these shapes, which Wacław Sierpiński [“VAHTS-wahf sher-PEEN-skee”] described in 1915. That shape is made by cutting a triangle into four smaller triangles and removing the middle one, over and over.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these shapes, such as the Koch snowflake, whose small parts look like the whole.

tossups.p: Folding a strip of paper in half over and over, then opening every fold to a right angle, traces out one of these shapes called the dragon curve. Martin Gardner introduced that curve to many readers in his “Mathematical Games” column in _Scientific American_.
tossups.r: In the song “Let It Go,” Elsa sings that her soul is spiraling in frozen examples of these shapes. For 10 points, name these self-similar patterns.

tossups.p: The box-counting method estimates the dimension of one of these shapes by covering it with smaller and smaller squares. Some cell phone antennas use these shapes to pick up many frequencies in a small space.
tossups.r: Their small parts look like the whole, a property called self-similarity. For 10 points, name these shapes with endless detail, named by Benoit Mandelbrot.

tossups.p: The strange attractor that Edward Lorenz found in 1963 while modeling the weather has the detailed, repeating structure of one of these shapes. Such shapes often appear in chaos theory, which studies systems that are very sensitive to their starting conditions.
tossups.r: Ferns and snowflakes have the self-similar look of these shapes. For 10 points, name these patterns studied by Benoit Mandelbrot.

tossups.p: Felix Hausdorff’s [“HOWS-dorfs”] 1918 definition of dimension gives many of these shapes values that are not whole numbers, such as about 1.585 for one built by repeatedly removing triangles. By that measure, a coastline counts as more than a line but less than a plane.
tossups.r: The florets of Romanesco broccoli show this pattern. For 10 points, name these self-similar shapes, which include the Mandelbrot set.

tossups.p: The most famous of these shapes contains every complex number c for which repeatedly squaring and adding c, starting from 0, never runs off to infinity. Its boundary is so wiggly that its Hausdorff [“HOWS-dorf”] dimension is 2, the same as a filled-in square.
tossups.r: That shape is named for Benoit Mandelbrot. For 10 points, name these shapes, whose small parts resemble the whole.

tossups.p: Physicist Richard Taylor argued in 1999 that the drip paintings of Jackson Pollock contain these patterns. In 1891, David Hilbert described a curve that winds through every point of a square, an example of these shapes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these never-ending, self-similar patterns, such as the Koch snowflake and the Mandelbrot set.

trap.title: The family or one member?
trap.body: Many tossups ask for one famous example instead of the whole family: the Mandelbrot set, a Julia set, the Koch snowflake, the Sierpiński triangle, or the Cantor set. Others want chaos theory, the field that studies systems like the weather, or Benoit Mandelbrot himself.
trap.fix: Listen to the giveaway: “these shapes” or “these patterns,” plus self-similarity or dimensions that are not whole numbers, means fractals. “This set,” with z² + c, means the Mandelbrot set; “this snowflake” means the Koch snowflake. Saying only “self-similar shapes” earns a prompt.

topics.name: Complex numbers
topics.kicker: Numbers of the form a + bi · A real part plus an imaginary part
topics.dates: First rules given by Rafael Bombelli, 1572
topics.briefing: A complex number joins a real number and an imaginary number, written a + bi, where i is the square root of −1. Mathematicians first ran into these numbers in the 1500s while solving cubic equations, and René Descartes dismissively called part of them “imaginary.” Drawn as points on a plane, they turned out to be essential for describing rotations, electric circuits, and quantum physics.
topics.answerHtml: complex numbers (accept complex; prompt on imaginary numbers; do not accept “real numbers”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: William Rowan Hamilton defined these numbers as ordered pairs of real numbers, and in 1843 he carved the rule for a four-part extension of them, the quaternions, into a bridge in Dublin. Multiplying one of these numbers by i rotates its point 90 degrees around the origin.
tossups.r: These numbers have the form a plus b i, where i squared equals negative 1. For 10 points, name these numbers with a real part and an imaginary part.

tossups.p: Rafael Bombelli’s [“bom-BEL-eez”] 1572 book _Algebra_ gave the first rules for calculating with these numbers. They had shown up as square roots of negative numbers when Gerolamo Cardano [“kar-DAH-noh”] solved cubic equations in his 1545 book _Ars Magna_.
tossups.r: René Descartes [“day-KART”] dismissively called part of them “imaginary.” For 10 points, name these numbers of the form a plus b i.

tossups.p: Caspar Wessel [“VESS-ul”] and, later, Jean-Robert Argand [“zhahn roh-BAIR ar-GAHN”] drew these numbers as points on a plane, with one axis for each of their two parts. Each one’s distance from the origin is its modulus.
tossups.r: One of these numbers, 3 plus 4i, has modulus 5. For 10 points, name these numbers that have a real part and an imaginary part.

tossups.p: Abraham de Moivre’s [“duh MWAHVZ”] formula raises one of these numbers, written using a sine and a cosine, to any whole-number power. Leonhard Euler’s formula lets each of these numbers be written using a distance and an angle, called its modulus and argument.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers of the form a plus b i, where i squared equals negative 1.

tossups.p: Because every polynomial that is not constant and has coefficients from this number system has a root in the system, mathematicians call it “algebraically closed.” Unlike the real numbers, these numbers cannot be put in order from least to greatest in a way that works with multiplication.
tossups.r: The quadratic formula gives two of these numbers when the discriminant is negative. For 10 points, name these numbers that combine a real part and an imaginary part.

tossups.p: Surprisingly, i raised to the power i is a real number, about 0.208, equal to e to the negative pi over 2. The powers of i repeat in a cycle of four: i, negative 1, negative i, and 1.
tossups.r: Numbers like 5 plus 2i belong to this larger number system. For 10 points, name these numbers that have a real part and an imaginary part.

tossups.p: Electrical engineers write the square root of negative 1 as j instead of i, because i usually stands for current, and they use these numbers to describe impedance in circuits. Wave functions in Erwin Schrödinger’s [“SHROH-ding-erz”] equation are made of these numbers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers of the form a plus b i, which can be drawn on an Argand diagram.

tossups.p: The Cauchy–Riemann [“koh-SHEE REE-mahn”] equations tell when a function of these numbers has a derivative, and a function with such a derivative at every point of a region is called holomorphic. Augustin-Louis Cauchy [“koh-SHEE”] also proved a theorem about the integrals of such functions around closed loops.
tossups.r: Each of these numbers has a conjugate, made by flipping the sign of its imaginary part. For 10 points, name these numbers, such as 4 minus 7i.

tossups.p: The Riemann [“REE-mahn”] hypothesis says that the nontrivial zeros of the zeta function, all of which are these numbers, have real part one-half. The roots of unity, which solve z to the n equals 1, are these numbers spaced evenly around a circle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers that include all the real numbers and all the imaginary numbers.

tossups.p: Carl Friedrich Gauss studied the examples of these numbers whose two parts are both integers, and he popularized the modern name of these numbers. His 1799 thesis proved that every polynomial that is not constant has a root among them.
tossups.r: To add two of these numbers, add their real parts and their imaginary parts separately. For 10 points, name these numbers of the form a plus b i.

tossups.p: The Mandelbrot set is drawn on a plane of these numbers, where it contains every one of these numbers c for which repeating z squared plus c, starting at 0, stays bounded. A plane of these numbers is often called an Argand diagram.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers, such as 1 plus i, that have both a real part and an imaginary part.

tossups.p: Multiplying one of these numbers by its conjugate always gives a real number. To divide by one of these numbers, you multiply the top and bottom of a fraction by the conjugate of the bottom.
tossups.r: For example, 3 plus 4i times 3 minus 4i equals 25. For 10 points, name these numbers of the form a plus b i.

tossups.p: Writing these numbers in exponential form leads to Euler’s identity, e to the i pi, plus 1, equals 0. The modulus of one of these numbers is the square root of the sum of the squares of its two parts.
tossups.r: These numbers have the form a plus b i. For 10 points, name these numbers, made of a real part and an imaginary part.

tossups.p: Engineers describe alternating currents with rotating arrows called phasors, which are really these numbers written with a size and an angle. On a graph of these numbers, the horizontal axis holds the real numbers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers that have a real part and an imaginary part, like 6 minus 2i.

tossups.p: Doubling the dimension of these numbers gives the quaternions, and doubling again gives the octonions, which John Graves and Arthur Cayley found in the 1840s. On an Argand diagram, the horizontal axis shows the real examples of these numbers.
tossups.r: The other axis shows multiples of i, the square root of negative 1. For 10 points, name these numbers of the form a plus b i.

trap.title: Complex, real, or imaginary?
trap.body: These numbers contain two smaller families that are separate answer lines: the real numbers (no imaginary part) and the imaginary numbers (multiples of i, with no real part). Other tossups want just the number i, the imaginary unit, or a tool built from these numbers, such as the Argand diagram, the conjugate, or the quaternions.
trap.fix: If the clues mention both a real part and an imaginary part, a + bi, or the Argand diagram, say “complex numbers.” Saying only “imaginary numbers” earns a prompt, so be ready to say “complex.” If the giveaway asks for “this number” whose square is −1, answer i.
trap.line: Real answer line: complex numbers (accept complex; prompt on imaginary numbers; do not accept “real numbers”)

topics.name: Normal distribution
topics.kicker: Symmetric and bell-shaped · About 68% of values within one standard deviation
topics.dates: First found by Abraham de Moivre, 1733
topics.briefing: The normal distribution is the bell-shaped curve that appears whenever many small, random effects add up, from heights to test scores. It is symmetric around its mean, and about 68% of its values fall within one standard deviation of the middle. Abraham de Moivre first found it in 1733, and it is often named for Carl Friedrich Gauss, who used it to describe errors in measurements.
topics.answerHtml: normal distribution (or Gaussian distribution; accept bell curve or normal curve; prompt on normal or Gaussian)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1733, Abraham de Moivre [“duh MWAHV”] found this distribution as an approximation for the number of heads in a very large number of coin tosses. Pierre-Simon Laplace [“luh-PLAHSS”] later proved an early version of the theorem that explains why this distribution appears so often.
tossups.r: Its graph is a symmetric bell shape. For 10 points, name this distribution, often named for Carl Friedrich Gauss.

tossups.p: In Francis Galton’s “bean machine,” balls bounce left or right off rows of pegs and pile up in bins in the shape of this distribution. Adolphe Quetelet [“keh-tuh-LAY”] found that the chest measurements of Scottish soldiers fit this distribution.
tossups.r: About 68 percent of its values fall within one standard deviation of the mean. For 10 points, name this symmetric distribution.

tossups.p: William Sealy Gosset [“GOSS-it”], who published as “Student” while working for the Guinness brewery, found a distribution that looks more and more like this one as samples grow larger. Squaring and adding independent variables with the standard form of this distribution gives a chi-squared distribution.
tossups.r: Its graph is symmetric, and its mean, median, and mode are all equal. For 10 points, name this probability distribution.

tossups.p: Germany’s old 10-mark banknote showed a graph of this distribution beside a portrait of the mathematician it is often named for. That mathematician used it in 1809 to describe errors in measurements of the positions of heavenly bodies.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this distribution named for Carl Friedrich Gauss, whose graph is a symmetric bell shape.

tossups.p: This distribution’s graph switches from curving down to curving up one standard deviation from the mean on each side. Its formula raises e to the power negative one-half times a z-score squared and divides by sigma times the square root of 2 pi.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this distribution, whose standard form has mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

tossups.p: The Six Sigma quality program, developed at Motorola in the 1980s, is named for a distance of six standard deviations on this distribution. The error function, written erf, is used to find areas under this distribution’s graph.
tossups.r: About 99.7 percent of its values lie within three standard deviations of the mean. For 10 points, name this probability distribution.

tossups.p: The central limit theorem says that the average of many independent random values tends to follow this distribution, even when the individual values do not. For a large number of trials, the binomial distribution can be approximated by this distribution.
tossups.r: Its graph peaks at the mean and is symmetric on both sides. For 10 points, name this distribution often named for Gauss.

tossups.p: Karl Pearson popularized this distribution’s usual name around 1900, though earlier writers had called it names like the “law of error.” Its skewness is 0, since its left and right halves are mirror images of each other.
tossups.r: Its mean, median, and mode are all the same. For 10 points, name this distribution, often named for Carl Friedrich Gauss.

tossups.p: Modern IQ tests are scaled so that scores follow this distribution with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15. Adult heights for men and for women each roughly follow this distribution.
tossups.r: About 68 percent of its values lie within one standard deviation of the mean. For 10 points, name this symmetric distribution.

tossups.p: James Clerk Maxwell showed that in a gas, each component of the molecules’ velocities follows this distribution. Teachers who “grade on a curve” sometimes assign letter grades to fit this distribution.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this distribution in which about 68 percent of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean.

tossups.p: Photo-editing programs often blur an image by spreading each pixel’s color according to this distribution. A table of z-scores lists the area under the standard version of this distribution’s graph to the left of each value.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this distribution, whose standard form has a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.

tossups.p: In Brownian motion, a particle’s change in position over a given time follows this distribution, with a variance that grows in proportion to the time. Many random measurement errors in science labs also follow this distribution.
tossups.r: Its mean, median, and mode are equal. For 10 points, name this distribution, which is shaped like a bell.

tossups.p: The highest point of the standard version of this distribution’s graph has a height of 1 over the square root of 2 pi, or about 0.4. Like every probability density, its graph encloses a total area of exactly 1.
tossups.r: Its graph never quite touches the horizontal axis. For 10 points, name this distribution named for Carl Friedrich Gauss.

tossups.p: If the logarithm of a quantity follows this distribution, the quantity follows a “log” version of it, which is often used to model stock prices. Adding up many small, independent random effects tends to produce this distribution.
tossups.r: Its graph is symmetric about the mean. For 10 points, name this distribution often named for Gauss.

tossups.p: The curve y equals e to the negative x squared has the shape of this distribution’s graph, and the total area under that curve is exactly the square root of pi. In this distribution, only about 3 out of every 1,000 values lie more than three standard deviations from the mean.
tossups.r: About 95 percent of its values lie within two standard deviations of the mean. For 10 points, name this probability distribution.

trap.title: Distribution or its measures?
trap.body: Many clues about this distribution, such as the 68–95–99.7 rule and z-scores, are really about the standard deviation, which is its own answer line, and so are the mean and the central limit theorem. Other distributions show up too: the binomial distribution counts successes in repeated trials, and Student’s t-distribution looks similar but has thicker tails.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This distribution” or “this curve,” with a symmetric bell shape, Gauss, or de Moivre, means the normal distribution. “This measure of spread,” written with the Greek letter sigma, means standard deviation; “this theorem” about averages means the central limit theorem.
trap.line: Real answer line: normal distribution (or Gaussian distribution; accept bell curve or normal curve; prompt on normal or Gaussian)

topics.name: Fermat’s Last Theorem
topics.kicker: No positive whole numbers solve aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ when n > 2 · Proved by Andrew Wiles
topics.dates: Stated c. 1637; proved by Andrew Wiles, 1994
topics.briefing: Fermat’s Last Theorem says that no positive whole numbers a, b, and c can make aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ true when n is bigger than 2, even though the n = 2 version, from the Pythagorean theorem, has endless solutions like 3, 4, and 5. Around 1637, Pierre de Fermat wrote in a book’s margin that he had a proof too big to fit. Andrew Wiles finally proved it in 1994, more than 350 years later.
topics.answerHtml: Fermat’s Last Theorem (accept FLT; prompt on Fermat’s theorem; do not accept “Fermat’s little theorem”)
reject: fermats theorem on sums of two squares

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Gerhard Frey suggested that a counterexample to this statement would produce a strange elliptic curve, and in 1986 Ken Ribet proved that such a curve could not be modular. That meant this statement would follow from the Taniyama–Shimura [“tah-nee-YAH-mah shih-MOO-rah”] conjecture.
tossups.r: Andrew Wiles proved enough of that conjecture in the 1990s. For 10 points, name this theorem that Pierre de Fermat scribbled in a margin.

tossups.p: Ernst Kummer [“KOOM-er”] proved this statement for every odd exponent that is a “regular” prime, a group that includes every odd prime below 100 except 37, 59, and 67. Kummer’s work on it introduced “ideal numbers,” an idea that became a key part of modern algebra.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theorem, finally proved by Andrew Wiles, which Pierre de Fermat claimed to have proved in a book’s margin.

tossups.p: Sophie Germain [“zhair-MAN”] proved a special case of this statement for prime exponents p for which 2p plus 1 is also prime. Adrien-Marie Legendre [“luh-ZHAHN-druh”] and Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet [“deer-ih-KLAY”] each proved the case where the exponent is 5, around 1825.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theorem about the equation a to the n plus b to the n equals c to the n, which went unproven for more than 350 years.

tossups.p: A prize of 100,000 marks for a proof of this statement, left by Paul Wolfskehl [“VOLF-skayl”] and announced in 1908, was finally awarded in 1997. According to a well-known story, Edmund Landau had cards printed to tell the many people who mailed him wrong proofs where their first mistake was.
tossups.r: That prize went to Andrew Wiles. For 10 points, name this theorem that Pierre de Fermat wrote in the margin of a book.

tossups.p: Leonhard Euler proved the case of this statement for cubes in 1770, though his proof had a gap. The case for fourth powers follows from a proof by infinite descent that no right triangle with whole-number sides has a perfect square as its area.
tossups.r: Its namesake, a 17th-century French lawyer, said his own proof would not fit in a margin. For 10 points, name this theorem proved by Andrew Wiles.

tossups.p: This statement was written next to a problem about splitting a square number into two other squares, in Claude-Gaspard Bachet’s [“bah-SHAYZ”] Latin translation of an ancient Greek book. It was first printed in 1670, five years after its author died.
tossups.r: That book was Diophantus’s [“dy-oh-FAN-tus-iz”] _Arithmetica_. For 10 points, name this theorem whose author claimed a “truly marvelous” proof, finally proved by Andrew Wiles.

tossups.p: In June 1993, a mathematician announced a proof of this statement at the end of a series of lectures at the Isaac Newton Institute in Cambridge, England. A gap turned up in that proof, and he fixed it in 1994 with help from his former student Richard Taylor.
tossups.r: That mathematician was Andrew Wiles. For 10 points, name this theorem saying that a to the n plus b to the n equals c to the n has no positive whole-number solutions for n above 2.

tossups.p: At age 10, a future mathematician found this statement in a library book by Eric Temple Bell and decided to prove it someday. He later worked on it in near secrecy for about seven years before announcing his proof.
tossups.r: That mathematician, Andrew Wiles, completed the proof in 1994. For 10 points, name this theorem that Pierre de Fermat claimed to have proved.

tossups.p: For proving this statement, a British mathematician received a special silver plaque in 1998 because, at 45, he was too old for a Fields Medal. He also won the 2016 Abel Prize and was knighted.
tossups.r: That mathematician was Andrew Wiles. For 10 points, name this theorem, which Pierre de Fermat wrote in a margin around 1637.

tossups.p: In a 1998 episode of _The Simpsons_, Homer writes an equation on a blackboard that seems to break this statement when it is checked on most calculators. A 1995 Halloween episode showed another near miss in a three-dimensional world.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theorem about whole-number powers, which Andrew Wiles proved in the 1990s.

tossups.p: In 2013, Andrew Beal raised his prize to $1 million for settling a more general version of this statement in which the three exponents may differ. With an exponent of 2, this statement’s equation has infinitely many solutions, such as 3, 4, and 5.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theorem that Pierre de Fermat claimed he could prove in a margin.

tossups.p: Simon Singh wrote a 1997 bestseller about this statement after making a BBC documentary on its proof. That proof depends on deep links between elliptic curves and objects called modular forms.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theorem that Pierre de Fermat wrote in the margin of a book, which Andrew Wiles proved.

tossups.p: Gabriel Lamé [“lah-MAY”] proved the case of this statement for seventh powers in 1839, but his 1847 attempt at a full proof failed because it assumed that certain numbers always factor in only one way. Joseph Liouville [“lyoo-VEEL”] pointed out that flaw.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theorem about the equation a to the n plus b to the n equals c to the n, which Andrew Wiles proved.

tossups.p: In a 1989 episode of _Star Trek: The Next Generation_, Captain Jean-Luc Picard spends his free time trying to prove this statement, which the show imagined would still be unsolved in the 24th century.
tossups.r: Five years later, Andrew Wiles completed its real proof. For 10 points, name this theorem that Pierre de Fermat claimed to have proved.

tossups.p: In Arthur Porges’s 1954 short story “The Devil and Simon Flagg,” a mathematician bets his soul that the Devil cannot prove or disprove this statement within 24 hours. The Devil fails but becomes obsessed with the problem.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theorem about a to the n plus b to the n equaling c to the n, which Andrew Wiles proved in the 1990s.

trap.title: Last, little, or the man?
trap.body: Pierre de Fermat has his own answer line, and tossups on him use the same margin, the same _Arithmetica_, and the same Andrew Wiles. Fermat’s little theorem (if p is prime, a^p − a is a multiple of p) is a completely different statement, and the Pythagorean theorem is the n = 2 case, which does have whole-number solutions.
trap.fix: “This theorem,” “this statement,” or “this conjecture,” with an equation like aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ, means Fermat’s Last Theorem; “this man” or “this lawyer” means Fermat himself. Saying only “Fermat’s theorem” earns a prompt, so add the word “Last.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Fermat’s Last Theorem (accept FLT; prompt on Fermat’s theorem; do not accept “Fermat’s little theorem”)

topics.name: Continuity
topics.kicker: No breaks, holes, or jumps · Drawn without lifting your pencil
topics.briefing: A function is continuous if you can draw its graph without lifting your pencil: no holes, no jumps, and no breaks. More precisely, at each point the function’s limit has to equal its actual value. Continuity is what makes calculus work, and it powers results like the intermediate value theorem, which says a continuous function can’t get from one value to another without passing through every value in between.
topics.answerHtml: continuity (accept word forms like continuous functions; do not accept “differentiability”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Karl Weierstrass [“VY-er-shtrahss”] made famous the epsilon-delta definition of this property, which says that keeping x close enough to a point keeps f of x within any chosen distance of its value there. Bernard Bolzano [“bohlt-SAH-noh”] gave an early version of that definition in 1817.
tossups.r: Informally, a function has this property if you can draw its graph without lifting your pencil. For 10 points, name this property of functions with no breaks, holes, or jumps.

tossups.p: Thomae’s [“TOH-mayz”] “popcorn function” has this property at every irrational number but lacks it at every rational number. The Dirichlet [“deer-ih-KLAY”] function, which equals 1 at rational numbers and 0 at irrational numbers, has this property nowhere.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property of a function whose graph has no breaks, jumps, or holes.

tossups.p: In 1872, Karl Weierstrass [“VY-er-shtrahss”] surprised mathematicians with a function that has this property everywhere but has a derivative nowhere. The absolute value function has this property at x equals 0, even though its graph has a sharp corner there.
tossups.r: Every differentiable function has this property. For 10 points, name this property of functions whose graphs can be drawn without lifting the pencil.

tossups.p: Bernard Bolzano [“bohlt-SAH-noh”] proved in 1817 that a function with this property on a closed interval hits every value between its values at the endpoints. By that theorem, a polynomial that is negative at one point and positive at another has a root in between.
tossups.r: That theorem is the intermediate value theorem. For 10 points, name this property of a function whose graph has no breaks or gaps.

tossups.p: In topology, a function has this property if the preimage of every open set is open. A homeomorphism [“hoh-mee-oh-MOR-fiz-um”] is a function with this property whose inverse also has it, which is why topologists treat a coffee mug and a doughnut as the same shape.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property of functions with no jumps or holes, which can be graphed without lifting a pencil.

tossups.p: The Heaviside [“HEV-ee-side”] step function, which jumps from 0 to 1 at x equals 0, lacks this property there. A function with this property on a closed interval must be bounded there, never shooting off toward infinity.
tossups.r: Polynomials have this property everywhere. For 10 points, name this property of functions whose graphs have no breaks.

tossups.p: The extreme value theorem says that a function with this property on a closed interval must reach both a maximum and a minimum there. Sums, products, and compositions of functions with this property also have it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property that a function has at a point when its limit there equals its value there.

tossups.p: L. E. J. Brouwer [“BROW-er”] proved that a function with this property from a disk to itself must leave some point fixed, as when stirred coffee keeps one point where it started. Points where a function lacks this property are called removable, jump, or infinite.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property of a function whose graph can be drawn in one unbroken stroke.

tossups.p: The Borsuk–Ulam [“BOR-sook OO-lahm”] theorem uses this property to show that at any moment, two opposite points on Earth have exactly the same temperature and air pressure, assuming both change gradually from place to place.
tossups.r: Its limit at each point equals its value there. For 10 points, name this property of graphs with no holes, jumps, or breaks.

tossups.p: In his 1821 textbook _Cours d’analyse_ [“KOOR dah-nah-LEEZ”], Augustin-Louis Cauchy [“koh-SHEE”] defined this property by saying that an infinitely small change in x produces an infinitely small change in the function. Bernard Bolzano had given a similar definition four years earlier.
tossups.r: A function with this property on an interval can be graphed without lifting your pencil. For 10 points, name this property.

tossups.p: The Weierstrass [“VY-er-shtrahss”] approximation theorem says that any function with this property on a closed interval can be matched as closely as you like by a polynomial. Every function with this property on a closed interval also has a definite integral there.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, which a function lacks at any hole or jump in its graph.

tossups.p: A function has this property at a point exactly when it sends every sequence approaching that point to a sequence approaching the function’s value there. The fundamental theorem of calculus is usually stated for functions that have this property.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property of a function whose graph has no holes, jumps, or breaks.

tossups.p: Rational functions have this property everywhere except where their denominators equal 0, and the tangent function lacks it wherever the cosine equals 0. The graph of 1 over x breaks apart at x equals 0, where it has a vertical asymptote.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property of a function that has no breaks, holes, or jumps.

tossups.p: A square table that wobbles on uneven ground can always be turned until all four legs touch, an argument that relies on this property of the ground’s shape. The function x squared minus 1, over x minus 1, lacks this property at x equals 1, where its graph has a hole.
tossups.r: Filling that hole with the value 2 would fix it. For 10 points, name this property of functions whose graphs can be drawn in one stroke.

tossups.p: Gottfried Leibniz’s “law” named for this property claimed that nature never makes sudden jumps. The floor function, which rounds down to the nearest integer, lacks this property at every integer, where its graph jumps like a staircase.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property of functions whose graphs have no breaks, holes, or jumps.

Its graph has no breaks, holes, or jumps
At a point a: f(a) is defined, the limit as x approaches a exists, and the two are equal

Every differentiable function has it, but not the other way around: the absolute value function has it at 0 despite its sharp corner
