Sums, products, and compositions of functions with it also have it
Rational functions lack it where denominators equal 0; 1/x breaks apart at x = 0; tangent lacks it where cosine is 0
Every such function on a closed interval has a definite integral there
Weierstrass’s 1872 function has it everywhere but has a derivative nowhere
Thomae’s popcorn function has it at every irrational number but not at any rational number
The Dirichlet function (1 on rationals, 0 on irrationals) has it nowhere
Topology: the preimage of every open set is open; a homeomorphism has it both ways, so a mug and a doughnut count as the same shape
The Heaviside step function, which jumps from 0 to 1 at x = 0, lacks it there; on a closed interval, a function with it must be bounded

Sequence definition: it sends every sequence approaching a to a sequence approaching f(a); the fundamental theorem of calculus assumes it
A wobbly square table on uneven ground can be turned until all four legs touch, if the ground’s shape has this property
Leibniz’s “law” named for it says that nature never makes sudden jumps

trap.title: Unbroken, not smooth
trap.body: Continuity and differentiability are easy to mix up. A function with a sharp corner, like the absolute value function at 0, is still continuous there but has no derivative there. Tossups also ask for tools built on this idea, such as limits, the intermediate value theorem, or the extreme value theorem, and each of those is its own answer line.
trap.fix: “No breaks, holes, or jumps” or “draw it without lifting your pencil” means continuity. “Has a tangent line,” “smooth,” or “has a derivative” means differentiability. If the question asks for “this theorem,” name the theorem instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: continuity (accept word forms like continuous functions; do not accept “differentiability”)

topics.name: David Hilbert
topics.kicker: German master of modern math · Posed 23 famous problems in 1900
topics.briefing: In 1900, at a big math conference in Paris, David Hilbert laid out 23 unsolved problems that kept mathematicians busy for the whole 20th century, and a few are still unsolved. From the German university town of Göttingen, he rebuilt geometry on careful axioms, dreamed up a hotel with infinitely many rooms, and worked on the equations of general relativity at the same time as Albert Einstein. His tombstone reads “We must know. We will know.”

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Paul Gordan grumbled that one of this man’s proofs was “not mathematics” but “theology,” because it showed that a finite basis must exist without actually building one. This man later proved the Nullstellensatz [“NOOL-shtel-en-zahts”], a theorem about the zeros of polynomials that underlies algebraic geometry.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German mathematician who presented a list of 23 unsolved problems in Paris in 1900.

tossups.p: This mathematician said that one must always be able to replace the words “points, lines, and planes” with “tables, chairs, and beer mugs,” since only the rules connecting them matter. His 1899 book _Foundations of Geometry_ rebuilt Euclid’s geometry on a complete, careful list of axioms.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German mathematician who imagined a fully booked hotel with infinitely many rooms.

tossups.p: In 1970, Yuri Matiyasevich [“mah-tee-yah-SEH-vich”] completed a proof that no general method can decide whether a polynomial equation has integer solutions, answering the tenth of this man’s famous problems. The first of those problems was Georg Cantor’s continuum hypothesis, about sizes of infinity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German mathematician who posed 23 problems at a 1900 conference in Paris.

tossups.p: Rejecting the motto “ignoramus et ignorabimus,” meaning “we do not know and will not know,” this man ended a 1930 radio speech in his hometown of Königsberg with a famous six-word reply. Around the same time, Kurt Gödel [“GUR-dul”] announced a result in that city that undercut this man’s hope that every true statement in math could be proved.
tossups.r: That reply is carved on his tombstone. For 10 points, name this German mathematician of the 23 problems, who declared, “We must know. We will know.”

tossups.p: In November 1915, this man presented his own work on gravity five days before Albert Einstein presented the final field equations of general relativity, and an “action” that leads to those equations is named for both men. This man had invited Emmy Noether [“NUR-tuh”] to help with questions about energy in that theory.
tossups.r: Infinite-dimensional spaces used in quantum mechanics are named for him. For 10 points, name this German mathematician who posed 23 famous problems in 1900.

tossups.p: In 1891, this man described a curve, built from smaller and smaller U-shaped paths, that in the limit passes through every point of a square. That space-filling curve, a variation on one by Giuseppe Peano [“pay-AH-noh”], also helps computers organize data about locations.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German mathematician who imagined a fully booked hotel with infinitely many rooms that can always fit one more guest.

tossups.p: This man’s student Max Dehn [“DAYN”] became the first person to solve one of this man’s famous problems, showing that two solids with the same volume cannot always be cut into flat-sided pieces and rearranged into each other. Polygons with equal areas, by contrast, always can be.
tossups.r: Dehn’s answer settled the third of the 23 problems this man posed in Paris in 1900. For 10 points, name this German mathematician.

tossups.p: This man declared that “no one shall expel us from the paradise that Cantor has created,” defending Georg Cantor’s work on different sizes of infinity against critics. The first item on this man’s famous list of problems asked whether any size of infinity lies between those of the counting numbers and the real numbers.
tossups.r: Infinite-dimensional spaces used in quantum mechanics are named for him. For 10 points, name this German mathematician who posed 23 problems in 1900.

tossups.p: In 1895, Felix Klein hired this man at the university where Klein taught, and together they made it the world’s leading center for mathematics. This man’s doctoral students there included Hermann Weyl [“VILE”], Richard Courant [“koo-RAHNT”], and Max Dehn [“DAYN”].
tossups.r: He also invited Emmy Noether to teach at that university. For 10 points, name this German mathematician who posed 23 problems in 1900.

tossups.p: This man’s program aimed to show that all of mathematics could be built on axioms that would never lead to a contradiction, checked with simple, step-by-step reasoning. Kurt Gödel’s [“GUR-dulz”] incompleteness theorems of 1931 showed that this program could not fully succeed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German mathematician whose name is given to the infinite-dimensional spaces of quantum mechanics.

tossups.p: Generations of physicists studied _Methods of Mathematical Physics_, a 1924 textbook this man wrote with his former student Richard Courant [“koo-RAHNT”]. That book turned out to contain many of the tools that the new quantum mechanics of Werner Heisenberg and Erwin Schrödinger [“SHROH-ding-er”] needed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German mathematician, the namesake of the infinite-dimensional spaces of quantum mechanics.

tossups.p: The sixth of this man’s challenges asked mathematicians to build physics on axioms, the way Euclid built geometry, and the eighth includes the still-unproven Riemann hypothesis. When this man first presented those challenges in a famous speech, he read aloud only ten of them.
tossups.r: The full list of 23 appeared in print. For 10 points, name this German mathematician who gave that speech in Paris in 1900.

tossups.p: George Gamow’s [“GAM-off”] 1947 book _One Two Three... Infinity_ popularized a thought experiment that this man had used in a lecture in the 1920s to show how strange infinite collections can be. This man also described a curve that winds through every point of a square.
tossups.r: In his thought experiment, a hotel with infinitely many rooms, all full, still has room for a new guest. For 10 points, name this German mathematician.

tossups.p: When other professors objected to letting a woman teach, this man fought for Emmy Noether [“NUR-tuh”], and for several years her courses were listed under his name. She had come at the invitation of this man and Felix Klein in 1915 and soon proved a theorem linking symmetries to conservation laws.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German mathematician who made Göttingen a world center of mathematics and posed 23 problems in 1900.

tossups.p: This man earned his doctorate in 1885 under Ferdinand von Lindemann, who had proved that pi is transcendental. As a student in his hometown of Königsberg, this man began a lifelong friendship with Hermann Minkowski [“min-KOFF-skee”], whom he later helped bring to his own university in 1902.
tossups.r: In 2000, seven Millennium Prize Problems were announced in Paris, a century after his list of 23 was presented there. For 10 points, name this German mathematician.

trap.title: Hilbert, Cantor, or Gödel?
trap.body: Clues about infinity and logic can point to three different people. Georg Cantor created the math of different sizes of infinity, Kurt Gödel proved the incompleteness theorems, and David Hilbert defended Cantor and launched the program that Gödel’s theorems undercut. A clue about an “action” named for “this man and Albert Einstein” can also tempt you to say Einstein, but the answer is the mathematician.
trap.fix: Hilbert clues: the 23 problems of 1900, Göttingen, the infinite hotel, Hilbert spaces, axioms for geometry, and “We must know. We will know.” Cantor clues: the diagonal argument and aleph numbers. Gödel clues: the incompleteness theorems (1931) and his friendship with Einstein at Princeton.

topics.name: The number one
topics.kicker: The multiplicative identity · Neither prime nor composite
topics.dates: Called the “unit” in Euclid’s _Elements_, c. 300 BCE
topics.briefing: One is where counting starts, and it has a superpower: multiply any number by 1 and nothing changes, so mathematicians call it the multiplicative identity. It is the only positive whole number that is neither prime nor composite, and any nonzero number raised to the zero power equals 1. It even stars in Euler’s famous identity, e^(iπ) + 1 = 0, alongside e, i, π, and 0.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Carl Friedrich Gauss used the seventeen complex 17th roots of this number to prove that a regular 17-sided polygon can be built with only a compass and straightedge. The complex nth roots of this number are evenly spaced around a circle and form the corners of a regular polygon.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this multiplicative identity, which leaves any number unchanged when you multiply by it.

tossups.p: Guido Grandi studied the endless series that alternately adds and subtracts this number, which seems to total 0 if you group the terms in pairs but this number itself if you group them differently. Grandi argued that the sum of that series was a half.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number, the only positive integer that is neither prime nor composite.

tossups.p: Alfred North Whitehead and Bertrand Russell’s _Principia Mathematica_ worked through hundreds of pages of logic before finally proving that this number added to itself equals 2. Euler’s [“OY-lerz”] identity says that e to the power i pi, plus this number, equals 0.
tossups.r: Multiplying any number by it leaves that number unchanged. For 10 points, name this number, the multiplicative identity.

tossups.p: In 1881, Simon Newcomb noticed that the first pages of books of logarithm tables were more worn than the rest. Benford’s law explains why: in many real-life lists of data, such as populations or prices, about 30 percent of the numbers begin with this digit.
tossups.r: This number is also the multiplicative identity. For 10 points, name this digit, the smallest positive integer.

tossups.p: About 1550 BCE, the scribe Ahmes [“AH-mess”] copied the Rhind [“RYND”] Papyrus, which writes fractions like two-fifths as sums of fractions with this number on top, such as a third plus a fifteenth. Ancient Egyptians wrote almost all of their fractions this way.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number, the numerator of every unit fraction, which is neither prime nor composite.

tossups.p: A whole number is “happy” if repeatedly adding up the squares of its digits leads to this number, as 7 does: 49, 97, 130, 10, and then this number. In binary, every power of 2 is written as this digit followed by zeros.
tossups.r: It is also the multiplicative identity. For 10 points, name this smallest positive integer, which is neither prime nor composite.

tossups.p: Lothar Collatz guessed that if you start from any positive whole number and keep halving even numbers, and tripling odd numbers and then adding this number, you will always eventually reach this number. In computer circuits and Boolean logic, this digit stands for “true” or “on,” while 0 stands for “false” or “off.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number, which equals 0 factorial and any nonzero number raised to the zeroth power.

tossups.p: Numbers called repunits, such as 11 and 111, are written using only this digit, and squaring the repunit 111,111,111 gives 12,345,678,987,654,321. This number fills the main diagonal of every identity matrix, which has zeros everywhere else.
tossups.r: Every whole number has this number as a factor. For 10 points, name this smallest positive integer, which is neither prime nor composite.

tossups.p: Harry Nilsson wrote a song, made a hit by Three Dog Night in 1969, that calls this number “the loneliest number that you’ll ever do.” A hydrogen atom has exactly this many protons, so hydrogen is the element with this atomic number.
tossups.r: Multiplying by this number leaves any number unchanged. For 10 points, name this number, which is neither prime nor composite.

tossups.p: Mathematicians define the empty product, the result of multiplying no numbers at all, to be this number, just as the empty sum is 0. Gottfried Leibniz [“LYBE-nits”] wrote an early explanation of binary, a number system that uses only 0 and this digit.
tossups.r: That is why 0 factorial equals this number. For 10 points, name this number, the multiplicative identity.

tossups.p: A classic argument notes that a third equals 0.333 repeating, so three thirds must equal 0.999 repeating, which is therefore exactly this number. The total area under any probability density curve, such as the bell curve, equals this number.
tossups.r: It is the probability of an event that is certain. For 10 points, name this number, the multiplicative identity.

tossups.p: Euclid’s _Elements_ defined a number as a “multitude composed of units,” so many ancient Greek thinkers did not count this quantity as a number at all. Some later mathematicians counted it as a prime, but it was eventually left out of the primes so that prime factorizations would be unique.
tossups.r: Multiplying by it leaves any number unchanged. For 10 points, name this positive integer, which is neither prime nor composite.

tossups.p: The Pythagorean identity says that the square of the sine of any angle plus the square of its cosine always equals this number. The sine of 90 degrees, the tangent of 45 degrees, and the cosine of 0 degrees all equal this number.
tossups.r: It is also the radius of the unit circle. For 10 points, name this number, the multiplicative identity.

tossups.p: The logarithm of this number is 0 in every base, and the natural logarithm of e equals this number. Adding a half, a fourth, an eighth, a sixteenth, and so on forever gives a total of exactly this number.
tossups.r: Any nonzero number raised to the zeroth power equals this number. For 10 points, name this number, the multiplicative identity.

tossups.p: Every row of Pascal’s triangle begins and ends with this number, and in the modern Fibonacci [“fib-uh-NAH-chee”] sequence, the two terms that come right after 0 are both this number. Multiplying any nonzero number by its reciprocal gives this number.
tossups.r: In Roman numerals it is written as I. For 10 points, name this smallest positive integer, which is neither prime nor composite.

trap.title: Adding or multiplying identity?
trap.body: Zero and one are easy to mix up. Zero is the additive identity (adding it changes nothing), while one is the multiplicative identity (multiplying by it changes nothing). Clues like “0 factorial” or “any number to the zeroth power” say “0” out loud, but the answer is the value they equal, which is 1. And don’t confuse one with i, the “imaginary unit,” which is the square root of negative one.
trap.fix: Ask whether the clue is about adding or multiplying: “unchanged when added” means zero, and “unchanged when multiplied” means one. If you hear “0 factorial” or “to the zeroth power,” answer with the result, 1. Saying “multiplicative identity” only earns a prompt, so be ready to name the number.
trap.line: Real answer line: one (or 1; accept unity; prompt on multiplicative identity)
